# Notation and a map of approximations {.unnumbered #sec-notation}

## Fields and thermodynamics

Symbols change roles between the stochastic and fluid chapters. Always read the local definition: $p$ may mean probability density, pressure, or single-particle momentum; $\rho$ may mean mass density or a quantum density matrix. Indices $i,j$ label spatial directions unless explicitly identified as state-space indices. Repeated spatial indices are summed.

| Symbol | Meaning | Useful units or qualification |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $n,\mathbf j$ | Number density and number current | $[n]=L^{-d}$, $[j]=L^{1-d}/t$ |
| $\rho=mn$ | Mass density in a one-species Galilean fluid | Distinct from a density matrix $\hat\rho$ |
| $\boldsymbol\pi,\Pi_{ij}$ | Momentum density and its flux | $\pi_i=\rho v_i$ only with suitable boost symmetry |
| $\epsilon,p,s$ | Internal energy density, pressure, entropy density | Rest-frame quantities unless stated otherwise |
| $T,\mu$ | Temperature and chemical potential | Often $k_B=1$ |
| $\chi$ | Static susceptibility | Commonly $(\partial n/\partial\mu)_T$ |
| $\mathbf v,\mathbf u$ | Fluid velocity or a specified drift | Check local convention |
| $D,\nu,\eta,\zeta$ | Diffusivity, kinematic/shear/bulk viscosity | $\nu=\eta/\rho$ for a simple fluid |
| $\kappa$ | Thermal conductivity, or a circulation quantum | Meaning stated in each chapter |
| $\sigma$ | Conductivity, noise amplitude, or surface tension | These are different quantities |
| $\Gamma,\tau$ | Relaxation rate and time | $\Gamma=1/\tau$ for a single exponential |
| $\phi,\theta$ | Superfluid phase or a scalar fluctuation | Defined where introduced |
| $\mathbf B,\mathbf E$ | Magnetic and electric fields | Electromagnetic unit conventions stated locally |

## Derivatives and transform conventions

The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+v_i\partial_i$. Vorticity is $\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf v$ in three spatial dimensions; in a two-dimensional flow its perpendicular component is often treated as a scalar. Do not confuse vorticity with frequency $\omega$.

Unless a chapter defines otherwise, perturbations have dependence $e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-i\omega t}$. Stable damping means $\operatorname{Im}\omega<0$. A growth rate $s$ in $e^{st}$ is related by $s=-i\omega$. With this convention a retarded response is Fourier transformed using $e^{+i\omega t}$ in the forward time transform; poles of stable retarded response functions lie below the real frequency axis.

The common mode types are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{diffusion:}\quad &\omega=-iDk^2+\cdots,\\
\text{sound:}\quad &\omega=\pm c_s k-i\gamma_s k^2+\cdots,\\
\text{relaxation:}\quad &\omega=-i\Gamma+O(k^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Only modes whose frequency vanishes at $k=0$ are strictly hydrodynamic. A gapped mode with small $\Gamma$ belongs in an enlarged quasihydrodynamic theory when the observation time is not much longer than $1/\Gamma$.

## Which approximation answers which question?

| Approximation | Typical condition | What must still be checked |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Hydrodynamic derivative expansion | $k\ell_{\rm micro},\omega\tau_{\rm micro}\ll1$ | All relevant slow variables retained |
| Local equilibrium | Microscopic equilibration faster than macroscopic change | Extra conservation laws, integrability, collisionless regime |
| Incompressible fluid | Small density variation; often low Mach number | Acoustic transients, imposed heating, boundary conditions |
| Inviscid bulk | Large Reynolds number, smooth interior flow | Boundary layers and singular gradients |
| Stokes flow | $\mathrm{Re}\ll1$; small unsteady inertia if neglected | Far-field matching and wall effects |
| Boussinesq fluid | Weak density variation, retained only in buoyancy | Stratification and thermal boundary conditions |
| Geostrophic balance | Small Rossby number away from singular regions | Equator, friction, time dependence |
| Dilute-gas Boltzmann closure | Binary short collisions and molecular chaos | Dense correlations, memory, quantum degeneracy |
| Relaxation-time collision model | A model spectrum for nonconserved modes | Conservation-preserving projection, coefficient accuracy |
| Ideal MHD | Negligible resistive effects on the time/length scale | Boundary fluxes, current sheets, reconnection |
| Kolmogorov inertial-range scaling | Scale separation, steady cascade, local isotropy assumptions | Intermittency, anisotropy, finite Reynolds number |

## Reconstructing a derivation when you get stuck

1. List the independent fields and their equilibrium values. State the spatial dimension and boundary conditions.
2. Write conservation equations before constitutive relations. Identify which coefficients need thermodynamics or microscopic input.
3. State the expansion: small amplitude, small gradients, small Reynolds number, or another parameter. These expansions are not interchangeable.
4. Check every retained term has the same units. Positive dissipative coefficients should damp stable equilibrium fluctuations.
5. Check the $k\to0$, zero-dissipation, and static limits. Compare the number of independent modes with the number of dynamical variables after constraints.

For detailed conventions in the source notes, use the original PDF linked at the top of the relevant lecture chapter. The [source guide](sources.qmd) describes how the source and companion differ.
